facts.claim: The essay (De Brevitate Vitae) is addressed to Paulinus ('my dearest Paulinus'). Seneca answers the common complaint that nature is stingy with life: 'It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste much of it.' Life is long enough and given in generous measure if all of it is well invested (1.3-1.4).

Analogy (1.4): wealth, however modest, grows with careful deployment when entrusted to a responsible guardian; vast wealth handed to a bad owner is scattered at once. Life, he says, extends if you know how to manage it.

What eats the days (2.1-2.2, 7): greed, drink, idleness, political ambition; people busy chasing other people's wealth or complaining about their own; days spent on ledgers, traps, bail, and dinner parties that have themselves become business. Death takes them by surprise.
3.1: people are thrifty in guarding their private property but let others trespass on their existence; they are most wasteful of the one thing it is right to be miserly with: time.

3.2: the audit. Seneca asks the reader to review his life, including how few days turned out as intended, and concludes the reader is dying before his time. 8.2: no one values time; all use it lavishly as if it cost nothing.

3.4-3.5: 'Your sort live as if you're going to live forever.' Plans are postponed to the fiftieth and sixtieth year. Seneca presents a hypothetical plan: 'After my fiftieth year I'll retire to a life of leisure; my sixtieth year will bring release from all my duties.' His answer: 'How late it is to begin living just when life must come to an end!' (Stewart renders the same as folly: to postpone sound plans to the fifty-first and sixtieth year and begin life at a point few have reached.)
9.1: 'The greatest impediment to living is expectancy, which relies on tomorrow and wastes today.'

Augustus (4.2-4.3): never ceased to pray for rest for himself and to seek release from the affairs of state; in a letter he spoke of his deep desire for that time, which he had long prayed for. 4.5: he had shed blood by land and sea, and plots were forming against him in the city itself.

Paulinus (18-20): Seneca urges him to withdraw 'to a more peaceful haven'. Paulinus manages 'the revenues of the world' and the public grain supply; the text does not give his office title. 19.1: retire to calmer, safer, more important pursuits. 20.1: those trappings of office are bought at the cost of life. 20.4: it is harder to obtain retirement from oneself than from the law.
Cicero (5.2): wrote 'I am lingering in my Tusculan estate, half-free'; Seneca says the wise man will never be half-free.
7.10: a man with white hair and wrinkles has not necessarily lived long, only existed long (Penguin-style and Basore translations; wording varies, 'grey hair' in some).
facts.source: Basore translation excerpt (thedailyidea.org); Braunstein quote; Williams 7.10 'not lived long but long existed'

facts.claim: 20.5: Seneca says such men's funerals should be held 'by the light of torches and wax tapers', as if they had lived briefly. 5.3: the wise man will never be half-free; he enjoys complete and unalloyed liberty.
9.1-9.2: you are arranging what lies in Fortune's control and abandoning what lies in yours; the whole future lies in uncertainty: live immediately.
facts.source: Stewart translation as quoted on philosophybreak.com and Goodreads quote collections; wording varies by translation

rejected.claim: Most people spend time on three things: answering others' demands, regretting the past, worrying about an unclear future.
rejected.reason: Not Seneca's list. His catalogue is greed, drink, idleness, ambition (f3).

rejected.claim: Seneca asks: 'How many days did you live for yourself? How many bent to others' agendas?'
rejected.reason: Close to the audit idea (f5) but not that wording; do not present as a quote.

rejected.claim: 'Life is not short, we make it short' as a pull quote with the old phrasing; 'give your own priorities a yes before others' urgent things'.
rejected.reason: The yes-to-priorities advice is not in the text.

rejected.claim: 'A good death is the reward of a good life, but a good life is lived daily, not on retirement day.'
Seneca does not see retirement as a goal; postponing life to retirement wastes most of life.
rejected.reason: Overstated. Seneca himself urges Paulinus to retire; his target is the person who postpones living, not retirement.

rejected.claim: Nightly ritual: 'What did I learn today? Which bad habit did I fight? Am I a better person?'
rejected.reason: That is the evening review in De Ira 3.36, not in On the Shortness of Life. Verified absent in the essay text.

rejected.claim: 'A life you do not account for is a life not lived' / 'What did I leave to future generations?'
rejected.reason: Not in the book. Invented attribution.

rejected.claim: Modern research shows daily reflection makes people happier and more productive.

1448.note: Postponement: Augustus's longed-for rest, the fifty/sixty plan, Paulinus.

1449.note: Core is the nightly self-review, which is from De Ira 3.36, not this book (verified absent). The audit-of-days passage that does exist is used in 1447.
